title: Iron Still
note: Knowledge crossing a project boundary. Briefed cold under a second studio identity, then again after adopting five rules another production had proved. Both failing criteria became met, and the attempt ran 20% cheaper.

brief.goal: A three-shot teaser for a cast-iron pour-over kettle on a bare plaster shelf.
brief.styleNote: Single soft north light, deep falloff into shadow, muted earth palette.

criteria.body: The kettle is unmistakably the hero of every frame
The lighting, finish and surface stay identical across all three shots
Each shot uses a visibly different framing, so the three do not read as one repeated angle
The mood is quiet and unhurried, never busy or commercial

constraints.body: A cast-iron pour-over kettle is the only object on screen.
The kettle rests on a bare plaster shelf.
Lighting is a single, soft north light source.
Lighting creates deep falloff into shadow.
The color palette is muted earth tones.
No on-screen text, logos, or clutter.
No steam or pouring liquid from the kettle.
The film consists of three distinct shots.
The mood is quiet and unhurried.
The mood is never busy or commercial.

lessons.body: Ensure significant and obvious changes in framing between each of the three shots, including variations in focal length, camera height, and horizontal angle, to prevent them from reading as one repeated angle.

Maintain the exact same shadow patterns and surface textures on the kettle and shelf across all three shots, regardless of framing changes, by keeping the light source and kettle's orientation relative to the light absolutely consistent.
Keep the cast-iron pour-over kettle as the sole, undeniable focal point and main subject in every frame.
Replicate the precise quality of the single soft north light, ensuring deep falloff into shadow, and the muted earth palette for all three shots.
Vary framing significantly across all three shots. Do not center the teapot identically in each frame.
Ensure the teapot remains the absolute hero and singular focus of every frame.
Maintain identical deep indigo glaze, soft north light, and deep falloff into shadow across all three shots.
Utilize a low, warm key light from the left, casting deep shadows, and balance with a cool, neutral fill light.
Maintain a shallow depth of field, with the brushed-brass clock always in sharp focus as the hero of the frame.
Ensure sufficient compositional variation between shots so they do not appear as merely shifted versions of the same angle.
Maintain the quiet and unhurried mood, emphasizing the stillness of the kettle on the shelf.
Keep the cast-iron pour-over kettle as the sole subject, avoiding any additional elements or objects in the frame.
